title: Monotone convergence
objectives: Use the monotone convergence theorem to swap a limit and an expectation.

screens.title: Capping a holding time
screens.prose: A holding time $X$ is exponential with mean 2 years. We cap it at $n$ years: $X_n = \min(X, n)$. The dashed curve is the density, scaled up by 10. Slide the cap.
screens.question: What do the means $E[X_n]$ rise towards, in years?

hints.text: The caps only grow, so the means only rise.
They close in on the mean of $X$ itself, 2 years.

feedback.correct: 2 years. Raising the cap changes $X_n$ only where $X > n$, and the chance of that falls fast.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch where the caption settles as the cap grows.

byKey.read: That is the value at $n = 10$. The means keep rising, though slowly.
byKey.ten: You gave the largest cap. The mean of $X$ is the limit, not the cap.

explain.text: $E[\min(X, n)] = \int_0^n e^{-t/2}\,dt = 2(1 - e^{-n/2})$. As $n \to \infty$ it tends to 2, which is $E[X]$.

screens.title: The monotone convergence theorem
screens.prose: If $0 \le X_1 \le X_2 \le \cdots$ and $X_n \to X$ almost surely, then $E[X_n] \uparrow E[X]$. This is the **monotone convergence theorem**. The limit $E[X]$ may be $\infty$.
screens.question: Which hypotheses do the caps $\min(X, n)$ satisfy?

options.text: They are non-negative and increase to $X$.

options.why: You reversed the direction. Raising the cap lifts $X_n$, so the sequence increases.
You assumed the cap eventually stops mattering. For any $n$, outcomes with $X > n$ stay capped, so only the limit equals $X$.

options.text: They are all below 10, a fixed bound.
options.why: You used the largest cap in the picture. The cap grows with $n$, so no single bound works.

hints.text: Check the sign and the direction of the sequence.
Raising the cap lifts the curve, never lowers it.
Non-negative and increasing is all the theorem asks.

feedback.correct: Non-negative and increasing to $X$, so $E[X_n] \uparrow E[X] = 2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The theorem needs a non-negative, increasing sequence.

explain.text: Each $X_n \ge 0$ and $X_n \le X_{n+1}$, and $X_n \to X$ everywhere. The theorem then lets the limit pass through the expectation.

screens.title: Summing the tail
screens.prose: A trader's order fills at each attempt with chance 0.2. Let $N$ be the attempt that fills. Then $N = \sum_{k \ge 0} \mathbf{1}_{\{N > k\}}$, and monotone convergence on the partial sums gives $E[N] = \sum_{k \ge 0} P(N > k)$.
screens.question: Here $P(N > k) = 0.8^k$. What is $E[N]$?

hints.text: This is a geometric series with ratio 0.8.
Its first term is $0.8^0 = 1$.

feedback.correct: 5 attempts. The sum of the bars is the mean. The tail-sum formula needs monotone convergence to swap sum and expectation.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sum the geometric series from $k = 0$.

byKey.start: You started at $k = 1$ and left out the first bar, $P(N > 0) = 1$.
byKey.p: You gave the fill chance. The mean number of attempts is its reciprocal.
byKey.one: You divided by 0.8. The sum is $1/(1 - 0.8)$.

explain.text: $\sum_{k \ge 0} 0.8^k = \dfrac{1}{1 - 0.8} = 5$, which is $1/0.2$. Each indicator is non-negative, so monotone convergence lets us swap the sum and $E$.

screens.title: Proof of monotone convergence
screens.prose: We prove $E[X_n] \uparrow E[X]$ for $0 \le X_n \uparrow X$. Two lines are flawed. The line bounding $E[X_n]$ below and the line taking the limit of $E[\varphi\mathbf{1}_{E_n}]$ may swap.
screens.question: Put the proof in order, a reason in each line. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Fix a simple $\varphi$ with $0 \le \varphi \le X$ and a constant $c \in (0, 1)$.
The sets $E_n = \{X_n \ge c\varphi\}$ increase to $\Omega$, because $X_n \uparrow X \ge \varphi > c\varphi$ wherever $\varphi > 0$.
Then $X_n \ge c\varphi\mathbf{1}_{E_n}$, so $E[X_n] \ge c\,E[\varphi\mathbf{1}_{E_n}]$ by monotonicity.
With $\varphi = \sum_k a_k\mathbf{1}_{A_k}$, $E[\varphi\mathbf{1}_{E_n}] = \sum_k a_k P(A_k \cap E_n) \to E[\varphi]$ by continuity from below (level 1).

So $L = \lim E[X_n]$ exists, because the means rise and stay below $E[X]$, and $L \ge c\,E[\varphi]$. Let $c \uparrow 1$, then take the supremum over $\varphi$: $L \ge E[X]$. Monotonicity gives $L \le E[X]$, so $L = E[X]$. $\blacksquare$
Since $X_n \to X$, we have $X_n = X$ for large $n$, so $E[X_n] = E[X]$ eventually.
lines.why: You assumed the sequence reaches $X$. The caps stay below $X$ wherever $X > n$, so they only converge.

lines.text: The sets $E_n$ decrease, so continuity from above gives $P(A_k \cap E_n) \to P(A_k)$.
lines.why: You used continuity from above. The sets $E_n$ increase, so the rule is continuity from below.

hints.text: Squeeze $L$ between $c\,E[\varphi]$ and $E[X]$.
The sets $\{X_n \ge c\varphi\}$ grow to the whole space, which allows continuity from below.
Order: fix $\varphi$ and $c$, the growing sets, then the two inequalities (either order), then the conclusion.

feedback.correct: Right. The proof pushes $L$ above every simple function under $X$, which is the definition of $E[X]$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. State the growing sets before you take a limit.

byKey.d1: You used a line that treats the limit as a value reached. Convergence is not equality.
byKey.d2: You used the wrong continuity rule for growing sets.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: The factor $c < 1$ makes the sets $E_n$ grow to everything. Continuity from below then moves each level set's chance to its limit, so $L \ge c\,E[\varphi]$ for every $c$ and $\varphi$.

screens.title: Fatou's lemma from monotone convergence
screens.prose: For any $X_n \ge 0$ we want $E[\liminf X_n] \le \liminf E[X_n]$. Define $Y_n = \inf_{k \ge n} X_k$.
screens.question: Why can we apply monotone convergence to $Y_n$?

options.why: You mixed up inf and sup. An infimum over a shrinking tail grows, and its limit is $\liminf$.
You assumed the sequence settles. Fatou is for sequences that need not converge.
You assumed what Fatou avoids. The point is to build an increasing sequence from any sequence.

hints.text: Compare $Y_n$ with $Y_{n+1}$: one infimum has fewer terms.
Fewer terms in an infimum give a larger value.
So $Y_n \le Y_{n+1}$, and the limit is the $\liminf$.

feedback.correct: Then $E[\liminf X_n] = \lim E[Y_n] \le \liminf E[X_n]$, because $Y_n \le X_n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether $Y_n$ rises or falls with $n$.

explain.text: $Y_n \le Y_{n+1}$ and $Y_n \to \liminf X_n$, so monotone convergence gives $E[Y_n] \to E[\liminf X_n]$. Since $Y_n \le X_n$, $E[Y_n] \le E[X_n]$, which gives Fatou.

screens.title: Edge case: an infinite limit
screens.prose: In the last lesson, the St Petersburg payout $X = 2^K$ capped at $2^m$ had mean $m + 1$. The capped payouts are non-negative and increase to $X$.
screens.question: What does monotone convergence say about $E[X]$?

options.text: It says nothing, because the means must stay bounded.
options.why: You added a hypothesis. The theorem needs only non-negative and increasing.

options.text: $E[X] = 11$, the largest mean on the chart.
options.why: You read the last bar. The theorem takes the limit over all $m$.

options.text: $E[X]$ is finite, because every capped mean is.
options.why: You passed finiteness to the limit. Each capped mean is finite, but they have no upper bound.

hints.text: Take the limit of $m + 1$ as $m \to \infty$.
It exceeds every number.
$E[X_m] \uparrow E[X] = \infty$.

feedback.correct: $\infty$. The theorem allows an infinite limit, so the rising means $m + 1$ give $E[X] = \infty$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The limit of $m + 1$ is not a finite number.

explain.text: $E[X_m] = m + 1 \uparrow \infty$, so $E[X] = \infty$ by the theorem. No finiteness is needed.

screens.title: Running the theorem downwards
screens.prose: Let $U$ be uniform on $(0, 1)$ and $X_n = \dfrac{1}{nU}$. Each $X_n$ decreases to 0 at every $U > 0$. A colleague applies monotone convergence the other way.
screens.question: What is $\lim E[X_n]$?

options.why: You ran the theorem downwards. A decreasing sequence needs $E[X_1] < \infty$, and here it is infinite.
You read one point of the curve. The mean is an integral over all of $U$.
You assumed a finite mean. The integral of $1/u$ near 0 diverges.

hints.text: Compute $E[X_1] = E[1/U]$ first.
$\int_0^1 \tfrac{du}{u}$ diverges.
$E[X_n] = E[X_1]/n = \infty$ for every $n$.

feedback.correct: $\infty$. The means stay infinite while $X_n \downarrow 0$, so the theorem fails downwards.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether $E[X_1]$ is finite.

byKey.b: Decreasing sequences need a finite starting mean.
byKey.c: A height at one point is not a mean.

explain.text: $E[1/U] = \int_0^1 u^{-1}\,du = \infty$, so $E[X_n] = \infty$ for every $n$ although $X_n \to 0$. A decreasing sequence needs $E[X_1] < \infty$ (level 2, next lesson).

screens.title: Both sums in code
screens.prose: Write `tail_sum_mean(p, terms)`, the partial sum of $\sum_k (1 - p)^k$, which tends to $1/p$. Then write `years_to_reach(d, g, r, frac)`: the first year $n$ at which the discounted dividends reach `frac` of the full value $d/(r - g)$. Raise `ValueError` when $g \ge r$.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: partial sums to 9 decimal places, whole-number years, and two cases that must raise `ValueError`.

hints.text: The first is a plain loop. The second adds one dividend per year until the target.
Year $k$ pays $d(1+g)^{k-1}/(1+r)^k$.
Loop with `while total < target`, add the next year's term, and count the years.

feedback.correct: Right. Partial sums of non-negative terms only rise, and monotone convergence says they reach the full value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the terms one at a time and test against the target.

explain.text: The partial sums rise towards $1/p$ and $d/(r - g)$, as monotone convergence promises. The first year at 39 of the full £40 is the 78th.

screens.title: A dividend stream
screens.prose: A share's dividends $D_k \ge 0$ have $E[D_k] = £2 \times 1.03^{k-1}$ in year $k$, discounted at 8% a year. Because each $D_k \ge 0$, monotone convergence gives $E\big[\sum_k D_k/1.08^k\big] = \sum_k E[D_k]/1.08^k$.
screens.question: Fill in the table.

rows: First year the partial sum passes £39

hints.text: The stream is geometric: first term £2 over 1.08, ratio $1.03/1.08$.
The full value is $2/(0.08 - 0.03)$. The partial sum is that times $1 - (1.03/1.08)^n$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the geometric sum, then solve for the first whole year.

byKey.r0c1: The full value is $2/(0.08 - 0.03)$. Each dividend grows at 3% and is discounted at 8%, so the denominator is the difference.
byKey.r1c1: The partial sum first passes £39 when $(1.03/1.08)^n$ drops below $\tfrac1{40}$. Round the solution up to a whole year.

explain.text: The stream is worth $\dfrac{2}{0.08 - 0.03} = £40$. The partial sum is $40(1 - (1.03/1.08)^n)$, which first passes £39 at $n = 78$. A stream that can turn negative needs dominated convergence instead (next lesson).

ideas: Monotone convergence: if $0 \le X_n \uparrow X$ almost surely, then $E[X_n] \uparrow E[X]$, and the limit may be $\infty$.
It swaps a sum and an expectation for non-negative terms. It proves the tail-sum formula and Fatou's lemma.
Run downwards it fails unless $E[X_1] < \infty$: $\tfrac{1}{nU}$ decreases to 0 but every mean is infinite.

formula.note: Further reading: Williams, chapter 5 (monotone convergence and Fatou).

summary.trap: The theorem needs a non-negative, increasing sequence. It does not run downwards.

quiz.prose: A game stops at the first head of a fair coin, so $P(N > k) = 0.5^k$ for $k \ge 0$.
quiz.question: What is $E[N]$?

byKey.start: You started at $k = 1$. The first term, $P(N > 0) = 1$, counts.

quiz.question: Which sequence has $E[X_n] \to E[\lim X_n]$ by monotone convergence?

options.why: You picked the moving spike. It is not increasing at a fixed $U$: it is $n$ for a while, then 0.
You picked a decreasing sequence. The theorem needs an increasing one.
You picked a sequence that changes sign. It is neither non-negative nor increasing.

feedback.correct: $\min(X, n)$ is non-negative and rises to $X$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a non-negative sequence that only rises.

explain.text: Only the caps are non-negative and increasing. The others fail one hypothesis.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac12$: swap the sum and $E$ by monotone convergence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sum the geometric series from $k = 1$.

byKey.first: You gave the first term only.
byKey.zero: You summed from $k = 0$ instead of $k = 1$, which adds the term 1.

quiz.prose: Non-negative $D_k$ each have $E[D_k] = 1$, with no discounting.
quiz.question: What is $E\big[\sum_{k \ge 1} D_k\big]$?

options.text: $\infty$: both sides are infinite, and the theorem allows that.
It is undefined, because the sum has no limit.
options.why: You treated infinity as missing. For non-negative terms the sum is always defined, possibly $\infty$.
You took one term. Every term counts.
You assumed later terms vanish. Each has mean 1, so none does.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up the means.

explain.text: $\sum_{k=1}^n E[D_k] = n \to \infty$. Monotone convergence gives $E[\sum D_k] = \infty$ too.
